practicalNote:
ACM is a service that issues and manages SSL/TLS certificates, integrating with AWS services such as CloudFront, ALB, and API Gateway so that HTTPS communication can be configured with minimal effort. The most common real-world scenario is enabling HTTPS for websites that use a custom domain. By issuing a public certificate from ACM for a domain obtained via Route 53 and attaching it to a CloudFront distribution or an ALB listener, HTTPS delivery — including automatic certificate renewal — is complete. As the expiration date approaches, AWS automatically renews the certificate, which structurally reduces the risk of expiration-related incidents and is the biggest advantage compared to managing certificates manually.

A key consideration when working with ACM is the region constraint of certificates. A certificate attached to an ALB must be issued in the same region as the ALB. On the other hand, because CloudFront is a global service, certificates attached to CloudFront must always be issued in us-east-1 (N. Virginia). Certificates issued in the wrong region cannot be selected from a CloudFront distribution, which is a common pitfall for beginners. ACM also distinguishes between public and private certificates: public certificates are used for internet-facing systems, while private certificates issued by ACM Private CA are used for internal systems.

CLF-C02 / SAA-C03 frequently ask questions like "Which service is used to enable HTTPS?" and "In which region must a certificate for CloudFront be issued?". The difference between DNS validation and email validation is also a common topic. DNS validation, when combined with Route 53, can fully automate the renewal process, which is why it is the recommended option in production.

Amazon API Gateway is a managed service for publishing and managing HTTP APIs, REST APIs, and WebSocket APIs. The most common use case in practice is building serverless APIs in combination with Lambda. Requests from the frontend are received by API Gateway, which handles authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and CORS at this layer before forwarding them to backend Lambda functions or services running on EC2. Because no server runs continuously, costs are kept low during periods without traffic, and the service automatically scales to handle sudden traffic spikes.

API Gateway offers two main types — HTTP APIs and REST APIs — which are chosen based on the use case. HTTP APIs offer low latency and low cost, providing basic features such as JWT authentication and CORS, making them the first choice for most modern web and mobile API workloads. REST APIs offer advanced features such as request validation, API key management, AWS WAF integration, and private APIs, making them better suited for enterprise use cases and APIs that require fine-grained control. WebSocket APIs are used for bidirectional communication such as chat and real-time notifications.

CLF-C02 / SAA-C03 typically ask questions such as "Which service serves as the entry point for serverless APIs?" and "Which service integrates with Lambda to provide APIs to the frontend?". CORS configuration, authentication methods (IAM authentication, Cognito Authorizer, Lambda Authorizer), and rate limiting / throttling design are explored more deeply starting from SAA-C03. Basic production security topics — such as avoiding leaving Access-Control-Allow-Origin set to wildcard (`*`), and not logging API keys or authentication tokens — are also commonly tested.

AWS App Runner is a managed service that lets you deploy web applications and APIs directly from a container image or a source code repository. Without separately configuring foundational components such as VPCs, load balancers, and Auto Scaling groups, simply specifying a container image provisions an execution environment with an HTTPS endpoint. In practice, App Runner is adopted for publishing small to medium-sized web apps and APIs where the operational overhead of ECS or EKS is unjustified, for containerizing internal tools, and for running prototypes in production.

App Runner trades operational simplicity for some constraints. Because its pricing model assumes continuous operation (charging for active vCPU and memory hours), a minimum baseline cost is incurred even during periods of no traffic. In contrast, Lambda + API Gateway architectures incur almost no charges when there are no requests, but they use a function execution model rather than a container execution model, which changes how the application must be structured. App Runner suits cases where you want to run a continuously running web server in a container but want to avoid the complexity of ECS, while Lambda + API Gateway suits cases where you want to run lightweight per-request processing serverlessly.

For purely static sites, an S3 + CloudFront architecture is superior to App Runner in both cost and fit.

Amazon Athena is a serverless analytics service that lets you run standard SQL queries against data stored in S3. There is no need to provision a database server in advance — just place data in S3, register table definitions in Glue Data Catalog or similar, and queries can be executed immediately. In practice, Athena is used for analyzing CloudFront and ALB access logs, auditing CloudTrail logs, performing ad-hoc investigation on business data accumulated in CSV or JSON, and exploring data in a data lake.

Athena pricing is based on the amount of S3 data scanned per query (a few USD per TB). Therefore, the design of data formats and partitioning is the central concern for cost optimization. Converting row-oriented formats such as CSV or JSON to columnar formats such as Parquet or ORC significantly reduces scan volume because only the necessary columns are read. Additionally, partitioning by frequently filtered keys such as date or region allows Athena to automatically skip scanning unnecessary partitions. A standard design pattern is to manage table definitions (schema and partition information) centrally in Glue Data Catalog and share them across Athena and other analytics services (Redshift Spectrum, EMR, etc.).

CLF-C02 / SAA-C03 ask about Athena as "a serverless service that allows SQL analysis of data in S3". Differentiation from EMR (managed Hadoop/Spark) and Redshift (data warehouse) is also a frequent topic. The standard division is: Athena for ad-hoc queries and small to medium-sized log analysis, EMR for large-scale batch processing, and Redshift for routine BI analysis. Remembering this segmentation makes judgment calls easier.

summary: Amazon Aurora is an AWS relational database service compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL.

practicalNote:
Amazon Aurora is a relational database service compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL, built on top of a distributed storage layer designed independently by AWS. Compared with RDS for MySQL / RDS for PostgreSQL of the same instance class, Aurora is said to have advantages in throughput, availability, and recovery time. In practice, it is adopted for workloads with continuous read and write activity, such as primary RDBs for web applications, SaaS backends, and database layers for business systems that demand high availability.

A defining characteristic of Aurora is the separation of the storage layer and the compute layer. The storage layer is automatically replicated across six copies spanning three AZs, providing data loss tolerance (writes continue with up to two copies lost, reads continue with up to three copies lost) and fast recovery times. Writes are processed by a single primary instance, while up to 15 Aurora Replicas distribute the read workload. For SaaS workloads with rapidly growing traffic or workloads with large demand fluctuations, Aurora Serverless v2 automatically increases and decreases compute capacity based on usage.

CLF-C02 / SAA-C03 frequently ask questions such as "Which RDS variant is MySQL/PostgreSQL compatible?", "What configuration is used to distribute read workload? (→ Aurora Replica)", and "What is the difference between Multi-AZ and Read Replica?". The exam centers on understanding that Multi-AZ is a standby configuration for availability (the standby cannot be used for reads), while a Read Replica is a replica for read performance (writes cannot be performed on it). It is also worth noting that Aurora is positioned as one of the options within RDS.

AWS Auto Scaling is a mechanism that automatically adjusts the number of resources in response to demand. The most widely used form is EC2 Auto Scaling (Auto Scaling Group), which uses CloudWatch metrics (CPU utilization, request count, custom metrics, etc.) as triggers to scale EC2 instances within a minimum, desired, and maximum capacity range. In practice, standard adoption patterns include placing Auto Scaling Groups behind an ALB to provide load distribution and automatic scaling for the web tier, reducing instance counts at night or on weekends to lower costs, and implementing self-healing configurations that automatically replace failed instances.

Beyond EC2, the AWS Auto Scaling brand provides cross-resource scaling management (AWS Auto Scaling Plans) for ECS services, DynamoDB read/write capacity, Aurora Read Replicas, and other resource types. Scaling policies include target tracking scaling (deciding scale changes based on metric thresholds), step scaling (incremental adjustments), and scheduled scaling (based on time of day or schedules). Auto Scaling and ELB (ALB / NLB) are designed together as a fundamental pair: ELB handles health checks and traffic distribution, and Auto Scaling handles capacity adjustments.

CLF-C02 asks questions such as "Which mechanism automatically scales EC2 instances based on load?" and "Which service is combined with Auto Scaling to achieve high availability? (→ ELB)". Distractor options often plant unrelated services such as "a service that takes storage backups" or "a service that provides DNS" — services from entirely different domains than scaling. Starting at SAA-C03, settings for minimum, desired, and maximum capacity, the design of Auto Scaling Groups spanning multiple AZs, and the distinction between target tracking scaling and step scaling are explored more deeply.

AWS Backup is a managed service that centralizes backup management across multiple AWS services. It allows backup policies (frequency, retention, cross-region copy settings) to be defined collectively as backup plans across supported services — RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, EFS, FSx, EBS, S3, Storage Gateway, and more — and executed automatically. In practice, consolidating backups (previously managed separately as RDS snapshots, EBS snapshots, and DynamoDB on-demand backups) under AWS Backup reduces operational overhead by enabling unified management of retention periods that satisfy compliance requirements, centralized audit logs of who restored what and when, and consolidated restoration testing.

Backup design centers on RPO (Recovery Point Objective: how much data loss is tolerable) and RTO (Recovery Time Objective: how long can recovery take). For workloads with short RPO (a few minutes or less), service-specific fine-grained backup features such as Aurora continuous backup or DynamoDB Point-in-Time Recovery are often used in combination. For disaster recovery (DR), the standard approach uses AWS Backup's cross-region copy feature to replicate backups to another region. Backups should not only be taken but also tested periodically to confirm that recovery is actually possible.

CLF-C02 asks questions such as "Which service centralizes backup management?" and "For what is backup frequency determined based on RPO/RTO?". Starting at SAA-C03, the focus shifts to AWS Backup's role within DR strategies (Backup & Restore / Pilot Light / Warm Standby / Multi-Site Active-Active), retention period design that aligns with compliance requirements (SOC / HIPAA / PCI DSS), and protection mechanisms such as deletion permission restrictions and Vault Lock.

practicalNote:
AWS Budgets is a cost management service that lets you set budgets for AWS costs and usage, sending notifications or triggering actions when thresholds are exceeded. Beyond alerts based on actual values, it supports alerts based on forecasted values (how much month-end spending will be at the current usage pace), allowing budget overruns to be detected during the month rather than only when receiving the bill. In practice, it is used to set a low monthly budget (e.g., USD 10) on a sandbox account to prevent learning-related cost incidents, to set per-service budgets on production accounts to detect sudden cost spikes in specific services, and to enforce organization-wide cost governance by combining with Organizations.

Budgets supports multiple types. In addition to cost budgets (amount-based) and usage budgets (hour / GB / transfer-based), it also supports coverage budgets and utilization budgets for Reserved Instances and Savings Plans. With Action-enabled Budgets (Budgets Actions), automatic responses are possible when thresholds are exceeded — such as attaching IAM policies to stop resource creation for specific users, or stopping specific EC2 instances. However, to avoid business impact from false triggers, validate behavior in a staging environment before enabling Actions in production. Cost Explorer handles cost analysis and trend tracking, while Budgets handles threshold-based monitoring and notification — this role separation is the key distinction.

CLF-C02 asks questions such as "Which service detects AWS overspending?" and "Which service can alert on both actual and forecasted values?". Distractor options often plant "Cost Explorer (analytics)" or "CloudWatch (metrics monitoring)". The respective scope of each service must be understood separately. Starting at SAA-C03, the distinction from Cost Anomaly Detection (which uses machine learning to detect cost anomalies), organization-wide budget aggregation via Organizations, and permission design for Action-enabled Budgets are explored in more depth.

AWS Config is a service that records the configuration change history of AWS resources and evaluates compliance based on defined rules. It continuously captures configuration snapshots of each resource (EC2 / S3 / IAM / security groups, etc.) and tracks who changed which item, when, and how, in chronological order. Using Config Rules (managed rules and custom rules), compliance conditions can be continuously checked — for example, "Is the public access setting of an S3 bucket disabled?", "Is the EBS volume encrypted?", "Are there any security groups that allow all ports from 0.0.0.0/0?" — with notifications or automated remediation triggered when violations are detected.

In practice, AWS Config is adopted for continuous evaluation of security baselines (CIS Benchmark / AWS Foundational Security Best Practices compliance), providing evidence trails during compliance audits, and detecting configuration drift (identifying where manual changes have diverged from the IaC-defined state). The difference from similar services: CloudTrail records "API call logs (who called which API)", while Config records "the state and change history of resource configurations" — a different area of coverage. CloudWatch is a monitoring service for "metrics and logs" and operates in yet another dimension from Config's role. For cross-account governance, the standard design uses Config Aggregator to consolidate records from multiple accounts and regions into a single account.

A common exam topic is distinguishing among three services — Config, CloudTrail (API call logs), and CloudWatch (metrics monitoring) — by clarifying what each one records. AWS CDK (Cloud Development Kit) is an Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool that lets you define AWS infrastructure using general-purpose programming languages such as TypeScript, Python, Java, C#, or Go. Code written with CDK (a CDK app) is internally synthesized (synth) into CloudFormation templates and deployed as CloudFormation stacks. In practice, CDK is adopted for standardizing complex resource configurations by extracting them into reusable Constructs (components), parameterizing per-environment differences (dev / staging / prod) to provision multiple environments from a single codebase, and consolidating Lambda function code and infrastructure definitions into a single language.

Compared with writing CloudFormation templates (YAML / JSON) directly, the advantages include IDE completion and type checking, the ability to express loops and conditionals using the syntax of a programming language, and the ability to incorporate best practices as code via reusable Construct libraries (L1 / L2 / L3 Constructs / AWS Solutions Constructs). On the other hand, directly editing a CloudFormation stack that was deployed via CDK without going through CDK breaks synchronization. As an operational rule, the principle that CDK-managed targets are modified only via CDK must be enforced. CDK itself is not charged for, but the created AWS resources incur normal charges. To avoid accidentally creating high-cost resources, it is recommended to enforce a PR review checkpoint.

CLF-C02 asks questions such as "Which option allows infrastructure to be managed as code?" and "Which tool generates CloudFormation to manage resources?". A common point of discussion is the differentiation among CloudFormation, CDK, and Terraform (a third-party tool). CDK should be remembered as "AWS's official IaC tool that supports general-purpose languages". Starting at SAA-C03, the focus shifts to stack-splitting granularity, the CDK Construct hierarchy (L1 = thin wrappers around CloudFormation resources / L2 = with safe defaults / L3 = bundled best practices), and deployment permission control for production environments.

AWS CloudFormation is an Infrastructure as Code (IaC) service that defines AWS resources declaratively as templates (YAML or JSON) and manages creation, updates, and deletion collectively in units called stacks. Templates can define virtually any AWS resource — VPCs, subnets, EC2 instances, IAM roles, RDS, S3 buckets, and more — and executing a stack provisions resources in a consistent order while resolving dependencies. In practice, standard patterns include provisioning stacks from the same template for each environment (dev / staging / prod), using change sets to verify changes before applying them to production, and using StackSets to deploy across multiple accounts and regions at once.

The advantages of CloudFormation include the fact that the resource configuration is retained in a repository as code, making change history trackable in Git; that the drift detection feature can detect configuration drift caused by manual console operations; and that the rollback feature can automatically revert to the previous state on deployment failure. Instead of writing templates directly, higher-level abstractions such as AWS CDK (writing IaC in general-purpose programming languages) or AWS SAM (serverless-focused) are also synthesized internally into CloudFormation. There is no charge for CloudFormation itself, but the created resources incur normal charges. Forgetting to stop them or mistakenly defining expensive resources can lead to cost incidents.

A typical real-world configuration where CloudFront is heavily used is the "S3 + CloudFront" static site pattern. HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images are placed in S3 and delivered via CloudFront in front. This setup eliminates the cost of a continuously running server during idle periods while delivering content with low latency to users worldwide. It is adopted across all scales — from personal portfolio sites to corporate campaign sites.

For dynamic applications as well, the common pattern is to place CloudFront in front, cache static assets (images, JS, CSS) at the edge, and pass only API requests through to origins (ALB or API Gateway). This offloads delivery of unchanging assets to the edge and concentrates origin processing on requests that actually require it.

Security and cost perspectives should also be kept in mind. CloudFront includes AWS Shield Standard automatically, providing standard, baseline protection against DDoS attacks. When combined with AWS WAF, application-layer protections such as IP address restrictions, rate limiting, and SQL injection mitigation can be applied at the CloudFront edge. For S3 origins, the standard design uses OAC (Origin Access Control) so that the S3 bucket is not exposed directly and accepts only access via CloudFront. On the cost side, charges are incurred per data transfer volume, HTTP request count, and per Invalidation (cache eviction), but a free tier provides 1 TB of data transfer and 10 million requests per month.

This data is used in post-incident security investigations, compliance audits, and operational troubleshooting. Enabling it across all regions is a security baseline, and combining it with AWS Organizations allows centralized management of events across multiple accounts.

CloudTrail events are roughly divided into three types. Management events (control plane operations such as EC2 instance launches and IAM policy changes) are by default viewable in the "Event history" for the last 90 days. By configuring a Trail, events can be stored long-term in an S3 bucket, exported to CloudWatch Logs, or analyzed via Amazon Athena.

name: Amazon DynamoDB
summary: A serverless NoSQL database. Provides fast reads and writes based on key design, and scales easily with growth in capacity and access.
oneLine: AWS NoSQL database that requires no server management.
useCases: App data with clear access patterns
examPoints: Managed NoSQL database

saaPoints: Design tables based on access patterns

practicalNote:
Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL database service provided by AWS. AWS handles server provisioning, OS patching, and cluster management, allowing developers to focus on table design and application code.

**The core of the design is access-pattern-driven**. DynamoDB identifies data using a partition key (PK) and an optional sort key (SK). Items with the same partition key are stored in the same partition, making Query operations over sort key ranges fast. Table design proceeds in the order of "first enumerate the access patterns, then express those patterns through the key structure". You do not take the RDB approach of normalizing first and then JOINing.

**The use of Query versus Scan** is an important optimization point. Query specifies the partition key and uses an index, so it is fast and low-cost. Scan sequentially scans the entire table, becoming slower and more expensive as data volume grows. Avoid frequent Scan operations in production environments; the standard design pattern is to create a GSI (Global Secondary Index) and resolve the problem with a Query.

**There are two capacity modes**. On-demand mode automatically scales according to access volume and does not charge for unused capacity. Provisioned mode requires you to specify RCU (Read Capacity Units) and WCU (Write Capacity Units) in advance, often combined with Auto Scaling.

**DynamoDB Streams** is an event stream feature that captures changes to the table (INSERT / MODIFY / REMOVE) in real time. By integrating with Lambda, you can implement event-driven processing such as replication, notifications, and aggregation.

**Access control via IAM** is granted at the action level (`PutItem` / `GetItem` / `Query` / `Scan`, etc.) rather than at the table level. Following the principle of least privilege, assign an IAM role to a Lambda function that allows only the necessary operations.

SAA-C03 asks about the design of GSI / LSI (Local Secondary Index), in-memory caching with DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator), DynamoDB Streams + Lambda integration patterns, and the criteria for choosing between DynamoDB and RDS.

practicalNote:
Amazon EBS (Elastic Block Store) is a **block storage** service that is attached to an EC2 instance. From the OS perspective, it is recognized as an ordinary disk drive, and data can be read and written by mounting a file system on it. EBS volumes must be located in the same Availability Zone (AZ) as the EC2 instance, and **cannot be attached across AZs**.

**The differences from object storage (S3) and file storage (EFS)** are frequently asked about. EBS is suited for high-speed I/O scenarios where it is attached to a single EC2 instance as a block device. S3 is accessed per object via HTTP API, so it cannot be used as a disk from EC2. EFS is a shared file system that can be mounted simultaneously from multiple EC2 instances.

**Volume types** are selected according to the workload. General purpose SSD gp3 is the most common choice and offers good cost efficiency. Provisioned IOPS SSD io2 is used for database workloads that require high IOPS. Throughput-optimized HDD (st1) suits large-volume sequential read/write workloads (logs, big data processing), and Cold HDD (sc1) is a low-cost option for infrequently accessed large volumes of data.

**Snapshots** are a feature that stores point-in-time copies of EBS volumes in S3. Users can perform the operation without being aware of the underlying S3 bucket. Snapshots use an incremental backup approach: after the initial full snapshot, only the changed differences are stored, making the process efficient. You can restore a new EBS volume from a snapshot or copy it to another region for DR purposes.

An important note: **even if you stop the EC2 instance, the attached EBS volume continues to incur charges**. Unused volumes will continue to generate costs unless they are explicitly deleted.

Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is an IaaS service that allows you to launch and manage virtual servers (instances) in the AWS cloud. By selecting an AMI (Amazon Machine Image), you can start an instance with the OS and initial software pre-configured.

**Instance types** are selected according to the workload. They are divided into families such as general purpose (M / T series), compute optimized (C series), memory optimized (R / X series), storage optimized (I / D series), and accelerated computing (P / G series / GPU). CLF asks for the basic understanding of "selecting a combination of vCPU count and RAM".

**Purchase options** are the key to cost optimization and are frequently asked about in both CLF-C02 and SAA-C03.
- **On-Demand**: per-second billing, no commitment, suitable for short-term unpredictable workloads
- **Reserved Instances (RI)**: up to 75% discount with a 1-year or 3-year commitment. Suited for steady-state workloads
- **Savings Plans**: a newer mechanism that applies discount rates equivalent to RIs more flexibly (regardless of instance type)
- **Spot Instances**: utilize AWS spare capacity at up to 90% discount. Subject to interruption risk. Suited for fault-tolerant distributed workloads (batch, ML training, etc.)
- **Dedicated Host**: occupy a physical server. Supports BYOL (Bring Your Own License)

**The combination of Auto Scaling and ELB** is the standard configuration for web applications. Auto Scaling increases or decreases the number of instances in response to traffic, while ELB (Elastic Load Balancing) distributes requests across each instance. This configuration requires a **stateless design** (no session information stored inside an instance), and the standard pattern is to externalize sessions to ElastiCache (Redis / Memcached) or DynamoDB.

From the perspective of the **shared responsibility model**, EC2 places the management of the layers above the hypervisor (OS / middleware / applications) on the user (the "security in the cloud" domain).

practicalNote:
Amazon ECS (Elastic Container Service) is a fully managed container orchestration service that runs and manages Docker containers on AWS. It is operated with the following components: task definitions (blueprints bundling container images, CPU / memory, network, IAM roles, log destinations, and so on), tasks (one or more container execution units launched from a task definition), services (logical units that maintain a specified number of tasks and integrate with ALB / NLB as needed), and clusters (logical boundaries that group tasks and services).

You can choose between two launch types: "ECS on EC2" and "ECS on Fargate". With the EC2 launch type, users manage the EC2 instances that serve as container hosts, allowing flexible instance type selection, the use of GPU / specialized instances, and cost optimization with Spot instances. With the Fargate launch type, container host management is abstracted away to AWS, and users only need to specify CPU / memory requirements. This reduces server management at the cost of a higher per-unit-time execution cost compared to EC2 with self-management.

The standard configuration in practice is a three-tier setup where ECS tasks are placed in private subnets and only an ALB placed in a public subnet is reachable from the internet. The standard design includes dynamic port mapping from ALB to ECS service, container log output to CloudWatch Logs, and automatic scaling of task count via Auto Scaling (based on CPU / memory / ALB request count). Tasks have two types of IAM roles: the "task execution role" is used by ECS itself for AWS API operations such as pulling images from ECR and outputting CloudWatch Logs, while the "task role" is used when the containerized application accesses AWS APIs (S3 / DynamoDB, etc.). Confusing the two is a common cause of permission incidents, so they should be clearly separated in the design.

Amazon EFS (Elastic File System) is a fully managed NFS (Network File System) file storage service that can be mounted and shared simultaneously by multiple EC2 instances and Lambda functions. From the OS perspective, it is mounted as an ordinary file system, allowing multiple clients to read from and write to the same files concurrently. Capacity grows and shrinks automatically based on usage, eliminating the need to provision storage in advance. The major difference from EBS is that by placing a "mount target" in each subnet across multiple AZs, EC2 instances in multiple AZs can access the same file system.

The storage classes have a two-tier structure: "Standard" (multi-AZ redundancy / standard for typical web and application workloads) and "One Zone" (single-AZ redundancy / lower cost / suited for development and testing), each combined with Infrequent Access (IA) lifecycle management that automatically migrates infrequently accessed data to a lower-cost tier. With Lifecycle Management, you can set rules such as "move to the IA tier if not accessed for 30 days", reducing costs for datasets with skewed access patterns. Throughput modes can be chosen from Bursting (auto-scales proportionally to capacity), Elastic, or Provisioned (explicitly reserved).

practicalNote:
Amazon ElastiCache is a service that provides Redis-compatible or Memcached-compatible in-memory caches / in-memory data stores in a managed manner. Because it holds data in RAM and supports sub-millisecond read/write latency, it is used to offload high-frequency access to relational databases (RDS) and NoSQL databases (DynamoDB) onto a cache to reduce database load and response latency. Two engine families are available: Redis-compatible (based on Redis OSS / Valkey) and Memcached, to be selected according to the use case.

The Redis-compatible engine provides rich data structures such as strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, and streams, as well as persistence (snapshot / AOF), replication, cluster configuration (sharding), pub/sub, and transactions. It is chosen for scenarios that require more complex data operations than a simple KV store, such as session management, ranking aggregation, messaging, and real-time leaderboards. The Memcached-compatible engine narrows the functionality to a simple KV cache but can deliver high throughput via multi-threading, making it suited for the use case of simply caching a large number of DB query results. The dichotomy is: choose the Redis-compatible engine when persistence or replication is needed, and choose Memcached for purely caching purposes that need to scale horizontally.

Typical use cases in practice include session stores for stateless web applications, query result caches for SaaS applications where "the same user opens the same screen repeatedly", rankings / real-time aggregation, rate limit counters, and inter-component coordination via pub/sub. Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) is an AWS managed load balancer service that automatically distributes incoming traffic across multiple targets (EC2 instances / containers / Lambda functions / IP addresses). It comes in four types: ALB (Application Load Balancer), NLB (Network Load Balancer), GWLB (Gateway Load Balancer), and CLB (Classic Load Balancer), to be selected based on the layer and use case. ALB targets HTTP / HTTPS (Layer 7) and supports path-based, host-based, HTTP header, and query string routing. NLB targets TCP / UDP / TLS (Layer 4) and is suited for workloads that require ultra-low latency, high throughput, or static IP addresses. GWLB is a service specialized in inserting third-party virtual appliances (firewalls / IDS / IPS), while CLB is a legacy general-purpose load balancer.

A typical configuration is to place an ALB in front of a group of EC2 instances spanning multiple AZs, combined with Auto Scaling, to ensure high availability and scalability for a web application. Health checks are performed per ALB target group, and instances that fail to respond are automatically removed. It is common to configure HTTPS listeners and associate ACM certificates so that TLS termination is performed at the ALB. In microservices architectures, it is widely adopted to associate multiple target groups with a single ALB and use path-based routing to dispatch /api to an API server, /static to static content, and the rest to a web server.

AWS Fargate is a "serverless" compute engine for running containers on Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS. With traditional ECS / EKS, users had to launch and manage EC2 instances as container hosts, but with Fargate, users no longer need to be aware of the EC2 instances that run the containers. When you specify vCPU, memory, and network settings in the task definition (or Pod definition), AWS automatically provisions the capacity and launches the containers. OS patching, host management, and capacity reservation become unnecessary, significantly reducing the operational burden.

The main differences between Fargate and the EC2 launch type lie in the billing model and the scope of management. The EC2 launch type charges per instance per unit of time, and idle capacity is also billed. Fargate charges per task based on vCPU, memory, and execution time, so charges are incurred only for what is needed per container. The cost tends to be lower than the EC2 launch type when resource utilization is high, and higher when it is low. SAA-C03 asks about which Fargate is suited for among patterns such as "always-on API", "short-running batch", and "irregular processing", and how to choose between Fargate and the EC2 launch type.

Typical use cases include serverless container execution for web APIs, short-running batch jobs triggered by CI/CD pipelines, machine learning inference container execution, and one-off execution of third-party images (OSS tools). The differentiation from Lambda lies in the constraints: Lambda has a maximum execution time of 15 minutes and per-function limits, while Fargate's strength is its ability to handle long-running processes and arbitrary container images. In the exam context, CLF-C02 asks questions such as "which service runs containers without managing EC2?" and tests whether you confuse the relationships among ECS / EKS / Fargate.

By combining the four elements of IAM users, IAM groups, IAM roles, and IAM policies, it controls "who is allowed to perform which operations against which AWS resources". IAM policies are written in JSON and specify Action (API operations to allow or deny), Resource (target resources), and Condition (additional conditions).

IAM roles are a mechanism for delegating permissions not directly to IAM users but to AWS services (EC2, Lambda, etc.), other AWS accounts, or external identity federation (SAML / OIDC). For example, when a Lambda function writes an object to S3, instead of hard-coding access keys in the function, you assign an IAM role with PutObject permission for S3 to the Lambda. This reduces the risk of access key leakage and also lowers the operational burden of key rotation.

IAM itself incurs no additional charges, but permission mistakes can lead to unintended resource creation or unintended API calls that result in billing incidents, so the importance of operational design is high.

Access control to KMS keys is performed by combining "key policies" and "IAM policies". Pricing is based on a combination of DB instance running time multiplied by instance type, storage capacity, backup capacity, and data transfer volume. Long-term commitment discounts via Reserved Instances are also available. In CLF-C02, a frequent topic is the division of responsibilities under the shared responsibility model (who handles patching and backups) when comparing self-managed databases on EC2 with using RDS.

Because it offers a SQL interface, existing BI tools and SQL clients can connect directly without modification.

Redshift Spectrum extends the service by enabling direct SQL queries against data stored in Amazon S3 without first loading it into Redshift, enabling integrated analysis across data lakes and the data warehouse.

Major use cases include building an enterprise data warehouse by aggregating large volumes of data collected from multiple systems, serving as the analytical backend for BI tools (Amazon QuickSight, Tableau, Power BI, and others), integrated analysis with Amazon S3 data lakes, and aggregating data for machine learning preprocessing. Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) is an object storage service provided by AWS. It stores files (objects) in buckets (bucket names are globally unique across AWS) and can hold any kind of data, including HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, videos, logs, backups, and data lake files. The standard Amazon S3 Standard class provides 99.999999999% (eleven nines) of object durability, with redundant storage across multiple AZs built in.

Major storage classes include S3 Standard for frequently accessed data, S3 Standard-IA (Infrequent Access) and S3 One Zone-IA for infrequently accessed data, S3 Intelligent-Tiering for data with unknown access patterns, and S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and S3 Glacier Deep Archive for archival storage. By configuring lifecycle policies, objects can be automatically transitioned to cheaper classes after a set period or deleted once no longer needed.

Typical use cases include static website delivery combined with CloudFront, long-term storage of logs, backups, and snapshots, data lake foundations integrated with Amazon Athena, Amazon EMR, and Amazon Redshift Spectrum, and serving as the output destination for various AWS services (CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, ELB access logs, and others). Pricing is composed of storage capacity multiplied by the storage class rate, request counts, data transfer volume, and lifecycle transition request counts. From a security perspective, Block Public Access is enabled by default, providing protection against unintended public exposure. When serving content through CloudFront, the recommended configuration uses Origin Access Control (OAC) to restrict direct access to the bucket.

AWS Secrets Manager is a managed service for securely storing, retrieving, and rotating secrets such as database credentials, API keys, OAuth tokens, and other secret information. Secrets are encrypted at rest using AWS KMS, and retrieval permissions can be controlled at a fine granularity through IAM policies. Application code retrieves secrets through the AWS SDK by calling an API (GetSecretValue), eliminating the need to write them in plaintext within code, environment variables, or configuration files.

A major feature is automatic rotation. For Amazon RDS, Amazon Redshift, Amazon DocumentDB, and Amazon ElastiCache, AWS provides Lambda function templates for rotation that can update secrets automatically on a defined schedule once configured. For arbitrary secrets, similar automatic rotation can be implemented by writing a custom rotation Lambda function. Version management of secrets is built in, so older versions remain referenceable for a period during rotation.

Typical use cases include retrieving RDS connection passwords from Lambda functions or ECS tasks, securely storing API keys for external SaaS integration, and centrally managing credentials used in CI/CD pipelines. Pricing is composed of a monthly fixed fee per secret and the number of API calls. Compared to AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, Parameter Store has a free Standard tier but lacks automatic rotation, while Secrets Manager is positioned as a paid service that includes rotation. AWS Shield is a managed service that protects applications on AWS from distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks. It is offered in two tiers, Shield Standard and Shield Advanced, with Standard automatically applied to all AWS users at no additional cost. For workloads that use edge and boundary services such as CloudFront, Route 53, AWS Global Accelerator, and Elastic Load Balancing, basic protection against network-layer (L3/L4) attacks such as SYN floods and UDP reflection attacks is always enabled.

Shield Advanced is a paid upper-tier plan that is used by explicitly registering protected resources (CloudFront distributions, Route 53 hosted zones, ALBs/NLBs, Global Accelerator, and Elastic IPs). It adds more advanced L3/L4 attack mitigation, Layer 7 attack defense (such as HTTP floods), 24/7 access to the AWS Shield Response Team (SRT) during attacks, cost protection against EC2, ELB, CloudFront, and Route 53 billing spikes caused by DDoS attacks, and bundled AWS WAF usage fees (for protected resources).

Typical use cases include standard DDoS protection for CloudFront + S3 / ALB delivery based on Shield Standard, as well as contracting Shield Advanced for large-scale public services that require advanced defense and 24/7 support. From a pricing perspective, Shield Advanced incurs a monthly fixed organizational fee with a one-year commitment, so individual developers and MVP-stage projects typically rely on Shield Standard. In CLF-C02, the differences between Shield Standard and Advanced, and the division of roles with AWS WAF (which provides rule-based defense at the application layer through Web ACLs) — Shield for DDoS protection and WAF for application-layer rules — are frequent topics.

Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) is a fully managed publish/subscribe (Pub/Sub) messaging service provided by AWS. When a publisher sends a message to a topic, the same message is delivered to all subscribers of that topic. Fan-out delivery, which simultaneously delivers a single message to multiple destinations, is a major role of SNS, and it is used as a foundation for loosely coupling components.

Subscriptions (delivery destinations) support a wide range of endpoints. Supported targets include Amazon SQS queues, AWS Lambda functions, HTTP/HTTPS endpoints, email, SMS (mobile phone short message), mobile push notifications (Apple, Google, and Amazon push notification services), and AWS Event Fork Pipelines. By using subscription filter policies, each subscriber can receive only messages with specific attributes from those sent to the topic.

Typical use cases include email notifications to operations staff from CloudWatch alarms, fan-out patterns that simultaneously deliver messages to multiple SQS queues, asynchronous event linkage between microservices, and push notification delivery to mobile applications. Pricing is composed of publish request counts, delivery notification counts, and data transfer volume, with usage-based rates that differ by delivery protocol (SMS has a higher unit price, while SQS and Lambda delivery have lower unit prices). In CLF-C02, the division of roles between SNS (Pub/Sub, push delivery to multiple subscribers) and SQS (queue-based, with each message consumed by a single subscriber), and the SNS + SQS fan-out configuration, are frequent topics.

name: Amazon Simple Queue Service
summary: A message queue service. Separates producers from consumers to stabilize asynchronous processing.
oneLine: A queue service that safely buffers messages waiting to be processed.
examPoints: Provides loose coupling through queues
Standard Queue and FIFO Queue are available

practicalNote:
Amazon SQS is a fully managed message queue service from AWS. By separating the side that sends messages to the queue (the producer) from the side that receives them (the consumer), it asynchronizes processing and loosely couples the system as a whole. Senders can dispatch messages without being aware of consumer availability, and receivers can retrieve and process messages at their own pace, providing a buffer against sudden load spikes. SQS offers two queue types: Standard Queue and FIFO Queue. Standard provides at-least-once delivery without strict ordering, while FIFO provides exactly-once processing with ordering guarantees.

In practice, SQS is used for asynchronous order processing, distributing work to Lambda, buffering retries during failures, and passing jobs between ECS tasks. The visibility timeout is an important concept in SQS: it is the period during which a message becomes invisible to other consumers after one consumer has retrieved it but before processing has completed (and the message has been deleted). If processing does not complete within the timeout, the message becomes visible again and can be retrieved by another consumer. This guarantees at-least-once processing, but it requires consumers to ensure idempotency.

Pricing is based on the number of API requests, with data transfer volume billed separately. Configuring a dead-letter queue (DLQ) allows messages that fail processing beyond a specified number of attempts to be moved to a separate queue for later investigation. In CLF-C02, the basic concept of SQS as a means of loose coupling through message queues, the distinction between Standard and FIFO, and the visibility timeout are frequent topics.

AWS Step Functions is a fully managed orchestration service that allows multiple processing steps to be defined as a workflow and executed with state management, retry control, conditional branching, and parallel execution combined. Following a definition called a state machine (written in Amazon States Language, a JSON-based DSL), it executes tasks such as Lambda functions, ECS tasks, DynamoDB operations, and SNS notifications sequentially or in parallel, tracking the success, failure, and output of each step as state.

In practice, Step Functions is used for batch processing that invokes multiple Lambda functions in sequence, approval flows, ETL pipelines, and orchestration between microservices. Compared to a configuration in which Lambda functions invoke each other directly without Step Functions, the advantages include visualization of the execution history of each step in the console, declarative definition of retry and catch handling on failure, and state management of workflows lasting up to one year. Two types are offered: Express Workflow (for short-duration, high-throughput use) and Standard Workflow (for long-duration use with state history retention), to be chosen according to the requirements.

Pricing is based on state transition counts for Standard, and execution time and request counts for Express, with the caveat that waiting steps are also subject to charges. A common pattern is combining Step Functions with EventBridge to enable scheduled or event-driven execution. In CLF-C02, the framing of Step Functions as a workflow orchestration service, its combination with Lambda for serverless architectures, and visualization of state transitions are frequent topics.

AWS Systems Manager (SSM) is a suite of services for integrated operational management of AWS resources and on-premises servers. Rather than being a single service, it is provided as a collection of multiple capabilities, including Parameter Store, Session Manager, Run Command, Patch Manager, State Manager, and Automation. By installing the SSM Agent on EC2 instances or on-premises servers, each server becomes a manageable target for these capabilities.

The most commonly used features in practice are as follows. Parameter Store manages configuration values, connection strings, and encrypted secrets in a hierarchical structure, allowing retrieval from Lambda or EC2 (it is cheaper than Secrets Manager and is well suited to configuration values that are not sensitive secrets). Session Manager provides terminal access to EC2 without SSH keys or open inbound ports, eliminating the need for bastion hosts. Run Command allows scripts or commands to be executed simultaneously against multiple EC2 instances and is used to automate routine operational tasks. Patch Manager handles OS patching, and State Manager manages configuration drift.

Pricing varies by capability, with the Standard tier of Session Manager, Run Command, and Parameter Store available at no cost (Advanced Parameter Store and on-premises management extensions are paid). AWS Trusted Advisor is a service that inspects an AWS environment across five categories — cost optimization, security, fault tolerance, performance, and service quotas — and provides improvement recommendations aligned with best practices. The checks are automatically executed based on items predefined by AWS, and the results can be reviewed by category in the management console. Representative check items include enabling MFA on the IAM root user, S3 bucket public access, unused EC2 Elastic IPs, low-utilization EC2 instances, and service quota usage.

The number of available check items differs depending on the support plan. Basic Support and Developer Support provide selected items in the security and fault tolerance categories (MFA on root account, S3 bucket permissions, public EBS/RDS snapshots, security group port openings, and others) along with all items in the service quotas category. Business Support and above provide all categories and all check items (refer to the official documentation for the latest count), with additional capabilities such as automated retrieval through the API and weekly improvement reports. In exam contexts, the point that the scope of checks varies by support plan is repeatedly asked, so it helps to remember that Basic and Developer cover some security and fault tolerance checks plus all service quota checks, while Business and above cover all items.

name: Amazon Virtual Private Cloud
summary: A service that creates logically isolated networks on AWS. Combines subnets, route tables, Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, and more.
oneLine: A service for building your own private network inside AWS.
useCases: Placing RDS and EC2 in private networks
examPoints: Subnets are created per Availability Zone
Control traffic with Security Groups and NACLs
Internet Gateway provides internet connectivity
saaPoints: Use subnets across multiple AZs for high availability
Use NAT Gateway for outbound traffic from private subnets
VPC endpoints optimize connectivity to AWS services

Do not place private resources in public subnets
practicalNote:
Amazon VPC is a service that creates a logically isolated network space (a virtual private cloud) within an AWS account. The address space is defined by a CIDR block (such as 10.0.0.0/16), within which multiple subnets (public subnets and private subnets) are partitioned and placed per availability zone. Routing between subnets is controlled by route tables, the exit to the internet is provided by an Internet Gateway, and outbound communication from private subnets is realized through a NAT Gateway. By combining these building blocks, a structure similar to on-premises network designs can be reproduced on AWS.

Communication control is performed in two layers: Security Groups (instance-level, stateful, allow-only rules) and Network ACLs (subnet-level, stateless, supporting both allow and deny rules). Security Groups define, in an allow-list style, where traffic may enter and exit an instance, while Network ACLs handle coarser control at the subnet level. The two are used together, with a common configuration combining fine-grained control via Security Groups and broader blocking via Network ACLs.

In practice, a typical design builds a three-tier web architecture on a VPC, placing the ALB in public subnets, EC2 or ECS in private subnets, and RDS in database subnets. To connect multiple VPCs, VPC Peering is used, while Transit Gateway aggregates multiple accounts and multiple VPCs, and VPC Endpoints (Gateway type or Interface type) provide private access to AWS services. Creation of the VPC itself, subnets, route tables, the Internet Gateway, Security Groups, and Network ACLs is free of charge, while charges accrue for NAT Gateways, VPC Endpoints, and data transfer. In CLF-C02, the division of roles among the basic VPC components (subnets, route tables, IGW, NAT, Security Groups, Network ACLs) is repeatedly asked.

AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall) is a managed firewall service that detects and blocks malicious requests against web applications based on rules. It evaluates requests such as SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), large volumes of requests from specific IP addresses, and access from specific geographic regions according to the configured rules. WAF does not operate on its own; instead, it is deployed by being associated with a protected resource such as CloudFront, Application Load Balancer (ALB), API Gateway, or AWS AppSync.

Three types of rules are available: managed rules (rule sets provided by AWS or AWS Marketplace partners), custom rules (where conditions are written by the user), and rate-based rules (which block based on request counts within a given time window). Managed rules include frequently used rule sets such as OWASP Top 10 protection, bot management, and protection against known malicious IPs, and basic protection can be initiated simply by enabling them. These are bundled as rule groups within a Web ACL (Access Control List), and the Web ACL is then associated with the protected resource.

Pricing is based on a combination of the number of Web ACLs, the number of rules, and the number of processed requests, with additional charges per managed rule group. The relationship with AWS Shield Standard should also be kept in mind: Shield Standard provides L3/L4 DDoS protection to all AWS users at no cost, while WAF handles rule-based defense at L7 (HTTP/HTTPS). Because the two cover different domains, using WAF together with Shield Standard is the baseline approach for protecting web applications. In CLF-C02, framings such as WAF as L7 web application protection, integration with CloudFront and ALB, and the ability to defend against SQL injection and XSS through managed rules are frequent topics.

oneLine: A service that traces where APIs and Lambda processes become slow.
examPoints: A distributed tracing service
Used to investigate performance issues
Plays a different role than CloudWatch Logs

AWS X-Ray is a distributed tracing service that visualizes the request paths and processing times of distributed applications. For serverless architectures such as API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB, or microservice architectures such as ALB → ECS → RDS, it records the path that a single request takes through each component, along with processing time (latency) and error information for each component. In the X-Ray console, the overall picture is visualized as a service map, and it becomes possible to track, on a per-request basis, which inter-service calls are slow and where errors are occurring.

To enable X-Ray, either the X-Ray SDK must be integrated into the application code, or the X-Ray tracing feature of the target service must be enabled. Major services such as Lambda, API Gateway, ALB, SQS, and SNS can send data to X-Ray simply by enabling tracing in the console. When the SDK is integrated, custom subsegments (for external API calls, DB queries, and the like) can be recorded, allowing bottlenecks to be identified at a finer granularity. The sampling rate can be configured to control the proportion of requests captured as traces, helping to manage costs.

It is important to organize the role differences with CloudWatch Logs. CloudWatch Logs aggregates text logs from individual services, while X-Ray visualizes the execution path and processing times of requests that span multiple services. During incident investigations, the two are commonly used together: X-Ray helps identify which segments are slow or failing, while CloudWatch Logs provides the detailed logs for the relevant segments. Pricing is based on the number of traces recorded and retrieved, with a fixed free tier each month. In CLF-C02, framings such as X-Ray as distributed tracing, its use for investigating latency in Lambda or API Gateway, and the difference in roles compared to CloudWatch Logs are frequent topics.
